lessons.title: Solve and Graph Inequalities
lessons.objective: I can solve an inequality and graph its solution set on a number line.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my work using the words solve, graph, solution, and substitute.

concept.heading: How do I solve an inequality and then graph it?
concept.intro: I solve an inequality the same way as an equation: use inverse operations to get the variable alone. But the answer is a range of values, so I show all of them on a number line.
concept.keyIdea: Solving & Graphing One-Step Inequalities. 1. Isolate the variable using inverse operations on both sides (same as equations). 2. Write the simplified inequality with the variable on the left (e.g. x > 5). 3. Graph the solution set on a number line with open/closed circle and arrow shading

worked.title: Watch me
lines: Solve x + 3 > 53. The inverse of adding 3 is subtracting 3.
I subtract 3 from both sides: x + 3 − 3 > 53 − 3, so x > 50.
The symbol > does not include 50, so I use an open circle at 50.
'Greater than' shades right. Check: x = 60 gives 60 + 3 = 63 > 53. True!
linesEs: Resuelve x + 3 > 53. La inversa de sumar 3 es restar 3.
Resto 3 en los dos lados: x + 3 − 3 > 53 − 3, así que x > 50.
El símbolo > no incluye el 50, así que uso un círculo abierto en 50.
«Mayor que» sombrea a la derecha. Comprueba: x = 60 da 60 + 3 = 63 > 53. ¡Verdadero!

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Solve x − 5 ≤ 8. What is the inverse of subtracting 5?
We add 5 to both sides: x ≤ 8 + 5, so x ≤ 13.
≤ includes 13, so we use a closed circle and shade left.
linesEs: Resuelve x − 5 ≤ 8. ¿Cuál es la inversa de restar 5?
Sumamos 5 en los dos lados: x ≤ 8 + 5, así que x ≤ 13.
El ≤ incluye el 13, así que usamos un círculo cerrado y sombreamos a la izquierda.

vocabulary.definition: Isolate the variable, then show the complete solution set on a number line.
vocabulary.example: x + 2 ≤ 7 → x ≤ 5; closed circle at 5, arrow left.

vocabulary.definition: To find the number that makes it true.
vocabulary.example: x + 3 > 10 → subtract 3 → x > 7 — any number greater than 7 works

vocabulary.definition: To show answers on a number line with circles and shading.
vocabulary.example: x > 7: open circle at 7, shade right — shows all solutions at a glance

vocabulary.definition: A number that makes the equation or inequality true.
vocabulary.example: x = 8 is a solution to x > 7 because 8 > 7 is true; x = 5 is not because 5 > 7 is false

vocabulary.definition: To put a number in place of a letter.
vocabulary.example: Substitute x = 5 into x + 3 > 10: 5 + 3 = 8, and 8 > 10 is false, so x = 5 is not a solution

vocabulary.definition: All the numbers that make the inequality true.
vocabulary.example: For x > 4, the solution set is every number greater than 4, such as 5, 6, 7, ...

vocabulary.definition: Two math actions that undo each other, like × and ÷.
vocabulary.example: To solve x + 3 > 7, use the inverse of adding 3: subtract 3 to get x > 4.

lessons.title: Equations and Inequalities Problem Solving
lessons.objective: I can model and solve real-world problems using equations and inequalities.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my reasoning using the words model, equation, inequality, and reasonableness.

concept.heading: Should I model this problem with an equation or an inequality?
concept.intro: To model means to write a real situation as math. I use an equation when there is one exact total, and an inequality when there is a limit or a range of allowed values.
concept.keyIdea: Modeling Real-World Scenarios with Equations & Inequalities. 1. Define the variable and units in the scenario. 2. Look for keywords: 'equals/is' (=) vs 'at least/limit' (≥, ≤, >, <). 3. Write the algebraic model, solve with inverse operations, and check in context

worked.title: Watch me
lines: Clue: 'A total divided equally among 4 people gave each $85.'
This has an exact total, so I use an equation. Let t be the total.
Divided among 4 to get 85 means t ÷ 4 = 85, so t = 85 × 4 = 340.
Check reasonableness: $340 split 4 ways is $85 each. That makes sense!
linesEs: Pista: «Un total repartido por igual entre 4 personas le dio $85 a cada una.»
Esto tiene un total exacto, así que uso una ecuación. Sea t el total.
Repartido entre 4 para obtener 85 significa t ÷ 4 = 85, así que t = 85 × 4 = 340.
Comprueba que sea razonable: $340 repartidos entre 4 son $85 para cada uno. ¡Tiene sentido!

together.title: Let's try together
lines: Clue: 'The lookout earned less than $50.' Equation or inequality?
'Less than' is a limit, so it is an inequality. Let e be the earnings.
'Less than 50' means e < 50. Is $30 a reasonable value? Yes.
linesEs: Pista: «El vigía ganó menos de $50.» ¿Ecuación o desigualdad?
«Menos de» es un límite, así que es una desigualdad. Sea e lo que ganó.
«Menos de 50» significa e < 50. ¿$30 es un valor razonable? Sí.

vocabulary.definition: Use an equation for one exact value or an inequality for a range of values in a real situation.
vocabulary.example: Exactly $20: 4x = 20. At most $20: 4x ≤ 20.

vocabulary.definition: To show a real-life situation with an equation or inequality.
vocabulary.example: 'Twice a number is 18' → 2n = 18 — the equation models the words

vocabulary.definition: A math sentence with an equal sign showing both sides are the same.
vocabulary.example: x + 8 = 15 — exactly one answer: x = 7

vocabulary.definition: A math sentence that compares two sides with <, >, ≤, or ≥.
vocabulary.example: x + 5 > 12 — many answers: x = 8, 9, 10, ...

vocabulary.definition: Checking if your answer makes sense.
vocabulary.example: If the problem asks for a number of people and you get x = −3, that is NOT reasonable

vocabulary.definition: A letter that stands for a number that is unknown or can change.
vocabulary.example: “5 less than a number is 12” becomes x − 5 = 12, where x is the variable.

vocabulary.definition: A limit in a problem that tells what values are allowed.
vocabulary.example: “You can spend at most $20” is a constraint: cost ≤ 20.

title: Budget Boundaries
mission: Plan a purchase with a limit. Solve an inequality, graph its solutions, and select a sensible whole-number decision.
investigate: Interpret x ≤ 15 as a budget limit. Does spending exactly 15 qualify?
If each ticket costs $3 and you have $15, write and solve 3t ≤ 15.
Distinguish an equation asking for an exact cost from an inequality setting a maximum.
create: Plan an event under a fixed budget. Write an inequality, solve and graph it, then explain why the practical ticket count must be a whole number.

support.explanation: Subtract 6 from both sides: x > 14 − 6 = 8. Graph: open circle at 8, shade right.
feedback: The boundary number is right, but the inequality symbol flipped. Adding or subtracting on both sides never changes the direction of the symbol.
An inequality has many solutions, not just one. Look at what the > symbol allows on either side of the boundary.
Not quite. Subtract 6 from both sides: x > 14 − 6 = ___.
hints: Solve it like an equation: x has 6 added to it. The > symbol just rides along.
Subtract 6 from both sides — the inequality symbol keeps pointing the same way when you subtract.
Compute 14 − 6 and keep the >. Then test: pick a number bigger than your result and check it makes x + 6 > 14 true.

support.explanation: Add 9 to both sides: x ≤ 3 + 9 = 12. Graph: closed circle at 12, shade left.
feedback: Not quite. Add 9 to both sides: x ≤ 3 + 9 = ___.
You found the right boundary, but the symbol turned around. Adding the same number to both sides keeps the original direction.
This names only the boundary value. The ≤ symbol includes that value and a whole range on one side of it.
hints: x has 9 subtracted from it. Undo that first; the ≤ symbol keeps its direction.
Add 9 to both sides. Adding the same number to both sides never flips the symbol.
Compute 3 + 9 and keep the ≤. Check by testing a value at or below your boundary in the original inequality.

support.explanation: Subtract 10 from both sides: x ≥ 25 − 10 = 15. Graph: closed circle at 15, shade right.
feedback: The boundary is correct, but the symbol was reversed. Subtracting the same amount from both sides leaves the direction alone.
An inequality describes a whole set of values, not a single one. Check what the ≥ symbol includes.
Not quite. Subtract 10 from both sides: x ≥ 25 − 10 = ___.
hints: What's being done to x? 10 is added. Plan the inverse operation before you look at the choices.
Subtract 10 from both sides; the ≥ stays exactly as it is.
Compute 25 − 10 and keep the ≥. Test your boundary value — it should make both sides of the original exactly equal.

support.explanation: Add 4 to both sides: x < 11 + 4 = 15. Graph: open circle at 15, shade left.
feedback: Not quite. Add 4 to both sides: x < 11 + 4 = ___.
You isolated x correctly, but the symbol changed direction. Adding to both sides preserves the original inequality symbol.
This is only the boundary. The < symbol points toward an entire range of values instead of one number.
hints: x has 4 taken away. Which operation puts that 4 back?
Add 4 to both sides — the < direction does not change when you add.
Compute 11 + 4 and keep the <. Check: a number just below your boundary should make x − 4 < 11 true.

steps: Inverse operation: Add 6 to both sides
Graph: Open circle at 20, shade right
support.explanation: The variable side shows + 6, so the inverse is to SUBTRACT 6, not add. Subtract 6 from both sides: x > 14 − 6 = 8. Graph: open circle at 8 (because > does not include 8), shade right.
hints: The inequality has + 6. To undo adding 6, do you add or subtract?
Subtract 6 from both sides: x > 14 − 6 = 8, then open circle at 8 and shade right.

support.prompt: A museum has some paintings. After adding 12, they have 45. Which equation models this?
support.explanation: 'Adding 12' to the original number gives 45: p + 12 = 45. Solve: p = 33.
feedback: Subtracting says the museum LOST paintings, but 12 were ADDED to what they had. Choose the operation that matches 'after adding 12.'
12p means 12 groups of p, which is multiplication. Re-read what actually happened to the paintings the museum already had.
Dividing would split the paintings into 12 equal groups. The museum did something different with the 12.
hints: The museum STARTS with an unknown number of paintings p, then 12 more are ADDED to reach 45.
'Adding 12' means the model joins p and 12 with a plus sign, and the total 45 goes after the equals sign.
Write the story in order: p, plus 12, equals 45. Which choice matches without switching the operation?

support.prompt: A detective needs more than 8 hours to finish the investigation. She has already worked 3 hours. Which inequality represents the additional hours h she needs?
support.explanation: 3 hours plus additional hours h must be more than 8: 3 + h > 8. Solve: h > 5.
feedback: The equals sign pins her total to EXACTLY 8 hours, but she needs more than 8. Keep the total 3 + h and swap in the comparison the story demands.
This compares the extra hours to 3, but 3 is the time already worked, not the goal. It is the total of both amounts that has to pass 8.
The 8 and the 3 have swapped jobs here. 8 is the total she must go past, and 3 is what she has already finished.
hints: There are two time pieces: the 3 hours already worked and the extra hours h. Together they must pass 8 hours.
'More than 8' means the TOTAL of 3 + h sits on the big side of a strict inequality — not an equals sign.
Combine first: 3 + h. Then compare that total to 8 using the strict 'more than' symbol. Which choice is built that way?

support.prompt: Which model is correct for: 'A number divided by 6 equals 7'?
support.explanation: Divided by 6 is n / 6. Equals 7 means = 7. So n / 6 = 7.
feedback: "Divided" means division, not multiplication.
That shows subtracting 6. The words say divided by 6.
Use division here, not addition.
hints: Spot the operation phrase: 'divided by 6'. That phrase gives you the symbol between n and 6.
Keep the sentence order — the number n comes first, then the division by 6, then 'equals 7'.
Write n / 6 on the left and 7 on the right. Which choice shows division rather than multiplying or adding 6?

support.prompt: A bus can carry at most 48 passengers. There are already 31 on board. Which inequality shows how many more can board?
support.explanation: 'At most 48' means the total must be ≤ 48. So 31 + p ≤ 48. Solve: p ≤ 17.
feedback: Your total 31 + p is built right — the symbol is the problem. 'At most' is a ceiling: can the bus legally leave exactly full? Pick the symbol that allows it.
An equals sign forces the bus to end up exactly full. Think about whether “at most” also allows a total below the limit.
Subtracting takes away the 31 riders who are already aboard. They belong with the new riders, not apart from them.
hints: The bus already has 31 riders, and p more may board — but the TOTAL cannot pass 48.
'At most 48' allows exactly 48 but nothing above it, so you need the symbol with the 'or equal' bar, not > or =.
Add the parts first: 31 + p. Then cap that sum at 48 with the 'at most' symbol. Which choice matches?

steps: Problem: A detective already found 8 fingerprints at the scene. After dusting more surfaces, she has 15 fingerprints in all. How many new fingerprints did she find?
support.explanation: The variable x is increased by 8, so you undo addition by subtracting 8 from both sides (the inverse operation), not by adding 8 again. x + 8 = 15 becomes x = 15 − 8 = 7. So she found 7 new fingerprints. Check: 7 + 8 = 15 ✓
hints: x is increased by 8. What operation undoes adding 8 — adding 8 again, or subtracting 8?
Subtract 8 from both sides: x = 15 − 8 = 7 new fingerprints.

support.prompt: Predict the test value for these settings.  Round to four decimal places if needed.
support.explanation: x ≤ 15; x = 6 qualifies. Closed circle at 15: the boundary is included.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

core.prompt: Is x = 5 a solution to x + 4 > 12?
choices: No, because 5 + 4 = 9, and 9 is not greater than 12
core.explanation: Substitute: 5 + 4 = 9. Since 9 > 12 is false, x = 5 is NOT a solution.
feedback: Your arithmetic is right, but then compare: is 9 actually greater than 12?
Comparing 5 with the 4 in the expression skips the actual test. Substitute 5 for x, simplify the left side, then compare that result with 12.
Comparing x directly with 12 leaves out the + 4. Substitute first, then compare the simplified left side with 12.
hints: 'Is 5 a solution?' means: substitute 5 for x and see whether the statement comes out TRUE.
Replace x with 5 and compute the left side completely. Then compare that result to 12 honestly — is it really greater?
Compute 5 + 4 first. Then ask: is that total greater than 12? Your yes-or-no needs the correct REASON attached to it.

core.prompt: Catch the Open vs. Closed Circle Mistake
steps: Inverse operation: Add 4 to both sides
Graph: Open circle at 13, shade right
core.explanation: The solving is correct: x ≥ 13. But the symbol ≥ means 'greater than OR equal to,' so 13 IS a solution and must be included. Use a CLOSED circle at 13 (not open), then shade right.
hints: Does the symbol ≥ include the boundary value 13, or leave it out?
≥ and ≤ use a closed circle; only < and > use an open circle. Here use a closed circle at 13.

core.prompt: A student solved 4n = 52 and got n = 13. Is the answer reasonable if n represents the number of notebooks in a box?
choices: Yes — 13 notebooks per box is reasonable
Yes — but only if n is a fraction
core.explanation: 4 × 13 = 52 ✓. 13 notebooks per box is a reasonable whole number answer.
feedback: Too many by what measure? A box holding 13 notebooks is ordinary. Reasonableness asks whether the number fits the situation, not whether it feels big.
48 comes from subtracting 4 from 52, but 4n means 4 times n. Multiplication is undone with division.
Notebooks are counted in whole numbers, and substituting the solution back into 4n = 52 works out exactly. No fraction is needed here.
hints: 'Reasonable' asks two things: does the math check out, AND does the number make sense for notebooks in a box?
Check the math first: multiply 4 by 13 and see if it rebuilds 52. Then judge whether that count fits a real box of notebooks.
Compute 4 × 13. Does it equal 52? Then ask: could a box realistically hold that many notebooks? Match your reasoning to one choice.

steps: Problem: Seven evidence lockers hold 84 case files in all, split equally. How many files per locker?
core.explanation: The variable f is multiplied by 7, so you undo it by dividing both sides by 7 (the inverse operation), not by subtracting 7. 7f = 84 becomes f = 84 ÷ 7 = 12. So there are 12 files per locker. Check: 7 × 12 = 84 ✓
hints: f is multiplied by 7. What operation undoes multiplying by 7 — subtracting 7 or dividing by 7?
Divide both sides by 7: f = 84 ÷ 7 = 12 files per locker.

steps: Inverse operation: Subtract 8 from both sides
Graph: Closed circle at 7, shade right
stretch.explanation: The inverse of subtracting 8 is ADDING 8, not subtracting. Add 8 to both sides: x ≥ 15 + 8 = 23. Graph: closed circle at 23, shade right.
hints: The equation has − 8. What is the inverse of subtracting 8?
To undo − 8, you add 8 to both sides: x ≥ 15 + 8 = 23.

stretch.prompt: A detective has a budget of at most $100 for supplies. She already spent $37 on gloves. Write an inequality for the remaining amount r she can spend, solve it, graph it, and name three possible values for r.
stretch.frame: Inequality: 37 + r ≤ ___. Solving: r ≤ ___ − 37 = ___. Graph: ___ circle at ___, shade ___. Three possible values: ___.
stretch.explanation: "At most $100" puts a cap on the total, so the model is 37 + r ≤ 100. Subtracting 37 from both sides gives r ≤ 63. Because "at most" allows the boundary itself, the graph is a closed circle at 63 shaded to the left, and amounts such as $63, $40, and $10 are all possible values of r.
hints: 'At most $100' caps the TOTAL: the $37 already spent plus the remaining amount r must stay within 100.
Model it as 37 + r ≤ 100, then subtract 37 from both sides. 'At most' means the boundary IS allowed — remember that for the circle.
Compute 100 − 37 to find r's boundary. Then choose any three amounts at or below that boundary as your example values.

steps: Problem: A parking lot holds at most 200 cars. There are 134 already. How many more can park?
Answer: Exactly 66 more cars can park.
stretch.explanation: 'At most' means less than or equal to, so the model should be an inequality: 134 + c ≤ 200. Solving: c ≤ 66. Up to 66 more cars can park, not exactly 66.
hints: The problem says 'at most 200.' Does that mean exactly 200 or up to 200?
'At most' requires ≤, not =. The correct model is 134 + c ≤ 200, so c ≤ 66.

stretch.prompt: Create two word problems about the same situation: one that requires an equation and one that requires an inequality. Solve both and explain why the models are different.
stretch.frame: Equation problem: ___. Model: ___. Solution: ___. Inequality problem: ___. Model: ___. Solution: ___. The models are different because ___.
stretch.explanation: The two models differ because the two questions ask for different things. An equation fits when the situation names one exact amount, like 'I saved exactly $45', so it has a single solution. An inequality fits when the situation sets a minimum or a ceiling, like 'I need at least $45', so a whole range of values works. Same story, different clue words, different symbol.
hints: Use the same situation twice: one question asks for an EXACT amount, the other sets a limit or a minimum.
Choose clue words on purpose: 'exactly' or 'in total' for your equation; 'at least', 'at most', or 'more than' for your inequality.
Pick a scene, like saving money. Write 'I saved exactly $__' for the equation, then 'I need at least $__' for the inequality. Solve both and compare.
